analysis.one_liner: Creates a right to sue federal officials in court for violating your constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee for over a year and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, you can sue a state or local police officer in federal court if they violate your constitutional rights, but the Supreme Court only allows a narrow slice of such lawsuits against federal officers. This bill would write the right to sue federal officials directly into law, letting people recover money damages from federal agents and other federal workers who violate the Constitution. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in December 2021 and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people harmed by federal officials — for example, people detained or searched by federal Border Patrol, immigration, or prison officers — would gain a clear, statutory right to sue for money damages when their constitutional rights are violated. Today the Supreme Court has recognized such suits only in a few situations [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Amends the civil-rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) so that it covers officials acting under 'authority of the United States' as well as state and local officials, creating a stated statutory right to sue federal officers for damages [S3].

The bill gives individuals a statutory cause of action against federal officials for constitutional violations, which the CRS summary notes currently rest on Supreme Court inference and exist only 'in certain situations' [S2].
The remedy is recovery of damages, so a person wronged by a federal officer could win compensation rather than only an injunction or disciplinary action [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies and the federal officers they employ would bear the cost of lawsuits and damage awards when officers violate constitutional rights, and taxpayers would ultimately fund settlements and judgments paid on behalf of federal employees.

drawbacks.text: Creating damages liability against federal officials exposes individual government workers — including those acting in good faith — to personal lawsuits, a concern that has made Congress reluctant to extend such remedies; the bill text does not lay out a qualified-immunity carve-out in the material provided [S3].
The remedy would increase litigation against federal agencies, and judgments would ultimately be paid with public funds, adding costs that taxpayers bear [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real gap: after decades of Supreme Court decisions narrowing 'Bivens' suits, people wronged by federal officers often have no court remedy at all, and a statutory right would close that gap. The costs — more litigation against the government and exposure for individual officers — are real but are the same trade-off Congress already accepted for state and local officials under Section 1983. The bill died without any committee consideration, so its design was never tested in hearings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sat there for about a year, was referred to a subcommittee on November 1, 2022, and then the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Hank Johnson (D-GA) introduced the Bivens Act of 2021 on December 8, 2021, with 11 original cosponsors listed on the bill [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced [S5].
On November 1, 2022 — nearly a year later — it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties [S5].
No further action appears in the record before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1].
The bill had 14 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies and their officers are better off because the bill died: they remain shielded from most constitutional damages suits, since the Supreme Court recognizes such suits only in a few narrow situations. People harmed by federal officers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson (D-GA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 8, 2021 and sent it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.what_they_did: Cosigned the bill at introduction; the bill finished with 14 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with authority to schedule committee action
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat from December 8, 2021 until the Congress ended.

against.name: House leaders
against.role: House majority leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on [S4]; with one chamber, one committee, and no votes in the record, the bill never reached a test of where members actually stood.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies and their officers
industries.note: The bill would have made federal officers financially liable in court for constitutional violations, as state and local officers already are. Its death leaves them with court-recognized immunity in all but a few situations, so the industry's interest ran against the people the bill would have served.

Without a statutory damages remedy, agencies avoid judgments and settlements, and taxpayers avoid the bill for officers' misconduct — while also leaving citizens without compensation when they are wronged.
